title: Human Evolution
summary: The evolutionary history of the human lineage over roughly seven million years, reconstructed from fossils, archaeology and genetics.

facts.label: Common misconception
facts.value: Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; both descend from a shared ancestor

age6_8.summary: How people slowly changed over millions of years from earlier kinds of ape.
age6_8.body:
A very long time ago there were no people [1].

There were apes living in Africa. Over millions of years, some of them slowly changed [1].

One big change was standing up and walking on two legs. That happened before brains got bigger [1].

Later, they started making tools out of stone [2].

People like us appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago, and then spread all over the world [1].

Humans did **not** come from chimpanzees. Chimpanzees are our cousins. We both came from the same older ancestor, long ago [1].

age9_12.summary: The seven-million-year story of the human lineage, told through fossils and DNA.
age9_12.body:
Human evolution is the story of how our species, *Homo sapiens*, came to exist [1].

## Cousins, not ancestors

A common mistake is thinking humans evolved from chimpanzees. We did not.

Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 8 million years ago. Since then both lineages have been changing. Chimpanzees are our cousins, not our grandparents [1].

## Walking came first

One of the biggest surprises in this field is the order of events.

People once assumed a big brain came first, and walking upright came later. The fossils show the opposite. Our ancestors were walking on two legs at least 4 million years ago, when their brains were still roughly chimpanzee-sized [1].

"Lucy", a famous *Australopithecus afarensis* skeleton from Ethiopia, is about 3.2 million years old. She walked upright, and her brain was small [1].

## Tools and brains

Stone tools appear in the record from about 3.3 million years ago, though that earliest date is debated. By 2 million years ago, toolmaking was clearly established [2].

Brain size increased substantially over the following two million years.

## Our species

The earliest fossils of *Homo sapiens* come from Africa and date to about 300,000 years ago. Our species then spread across the world [1].

## Meeting other humans

We were not the only human species. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia, and Denisovans in Asia.

DNA recovered from ancient bones shows that our ancestors met and had children with them. Most people whose ancestors came from outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA today [3].

## Not a ladder

Evolution is often drawn as a line of figures becoming gradually more upright. That picture is wrong. Human evolution is a branching bush, with many species alive at the same time, most of which left no descendants [1].

teen.summary: The evolutionary history of the hominin lineage over approximately seven million years, reconstructed from palaeoanthropology, archaeology and ancient genomics.
teen.body:
Human evolution describes the divergence and development of the hominin lineage since its separation from the lineage leading to chimpanzees [1].

## Phylogenetic position

Humans and chimpanzees share a last common ancestor dated by molecular clock methods to roughly 6 to 8 million years ago. The frequent claim that humans descend from chimpanzees is a category error: both lineages have evolved independently since divergence, and the common ancestor resembled neither living species [1].

## Bipedality precedes encephalisation

The sequence of major adaptations is well established and runs counter to earlier expectations.

Bipedal locomotion is evidenced from at least 4 million years ago in *Australopithecus*, and possibly earlier. The Laetoli footprints in Tanzania, dated to about 3.6 million years, record a bipedal gait directly. *Australopithecus afarensis*, including the specimen known as Lucy, combined habitual bipedality with an endocranial volume in the chimpanzee range [1].

Substantial brain expansion follows considerably later, principally within the genus *Homo* over the last two million years. The "brain first" model — which motivated acceptance of the Piltdown forgery — was falsified by the australopithecine fossil record [1].

## Technology

Oldowan flaked stone tools appear by about 2.6 million years ago. Older tools from Lomekwi in Kenya, dated to approximately 3.3 million years, have been reported; their status is contested within the field, and they should be presented as a disputed claim rather than an established date [2].

Acheulean handaxes, hearth evidence for controlled fire, and eventually blade technologies mark subsequent developments.

## Origin of Homo sapiens

The earliest fossils attributed to *Homo sapiens* come from Africa. Material from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to approximately 300,000 years ago, extended the accepted age and broadened the geographic picture [1].

The emerging model describes African origins as structured across multiple interconnected populations rather than a single ancestral region — a revision driven by both fossil and genomic evidence.

## Interbreeding with other hominins

Sequencing of ancient DNA transformed the field. The Neanderthal genome, published in 2010, established that anatomically modern humans and Neanderthals interbred. Individuals with ancestry outside sub-Saharan Africa typically carry approximately 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal-derived DNA [3].

The Denisovans were identified from a finger bone in Siberia primarily through genomic rather than morphological analysis — a species effectively discovered by sequencing. Denisovan ancestry is elevated in populations in Oceania [3].

## Structure of the record

The familiar linear progression illustration is misleading. Multiple hominin species coexisted for most of the last several million years, and the majority of branches are extinct without descendants. *Homo sapiens* being currently the only surviving hominin is unusual, not the normal condition [1].

adult.summary: The evolutionary history of the hominin clade over roughly seven million years, integrating palaeoanthropological, archaeological and palaeogenomic evidence.
adult.body:
Human evolution concerns the phylogenetic and adaptive history of the hominin clade following divergence from the panin lineage [1].

## Divergence and phylogeny

Molecular clock estimates place the human-chimpanzee last common ancestor at approximately 6 to 8 million years ago, with the range reflecting genuine uncertainty in mutation rate calibration and generation time. Late Miocene candidate taxa including *Sahelanthropus*, *Orrorin* and *Ardipithecus* fall near this interval; their phylogenetic placement relative to the hominin stem is disputed [1].

The common assertion of descent from chimpanzees misconstrues cladogenesis. Both lineages are equally derived from a common ancestor that possessed the plesiomorphic character states of neither.

## Locomotor and cranial evolution

Habitual terrestrial bipedality is documented from at least 4 Ma and is the earliest well-attested hominin autapomorphy. Postcranial evidence from *Australopithecus afarensis*, together with the Laetoli trackway at approximately 3.66 Ma, establishes bipedal gait while endocranial volume remained within the extant chimpanzee range [1].

Encephalisation is substantially later, concentrated in *Homo* over the last two million years, with modern human endocranial volume averaging approximately 1,350 cm³.

That locomotor reorganisation preceded brain expansion is one of the more consequential corrections in the history of the discipline. The prior expectation of cerebral primacy contributed materially to the uncritical acceptance of the Piltdown forgery, which combined a modern cranium with an orangutan mandible and was not exposed until 1953 [1].

## Lithic technology

Oldowan industries are securely dated from approximately 2.6 Ma. Purported Lomekwian artefacts from West Turkana at approximately 3.3 Ma would substantially predate the genus *Homo*; the attribution has been questioned on taphonomic and contextual grounds and remains contested rather than accepted [2].

The Acheulean, with its bifacial handaxes, persists with remarkable morphological conservatism for over a million years — a stability that is itself an unexplained feature of the record.

## Origins of Homo sapiens

Fossils assigned to early *H. sapiens* include the Jebel Irhoud material from Morocco at approximately 315 ka, which extended the temporal range and displaced an exclusively East African model of origins [1].

Current synthesis favours African multiregionalism, or pan-African structured populations: modern human morphology and behaviour assembled in a mosaic across interconnected populations rather than emerging in a single locale. The model is supported by both fossil distribution and genomic inference of deep population structure.

## Palaeogenomics and admixture

Recovery of ancient DNA has reorganised the field. Publication of the draft Neanderthal genome in 2010 demonstrated introgression into non-African modern human populations, with present-day genomic contributions of approximately 1 to 2 percent [3].

The Denisovans were defined principally from genomic data recovered from fragmentary remains at Denisova Cave — a taxon characterised by sequence before morphology. Denisovan introgression is elevated in Oceanian populations, and specific introgressed alleles, including the *EPAS1* variant associated with high-altitude adaptation in Tibetan populations, have documented functional consequences [3].

The resulting picture is one of a braided rather than strictly branching phylogeny, in which reticulation between hominin populations was recurrent.

## Structure of inference

The iconic progressive-march illustration misrepresents the evidence in two respects: it implies anagenetic linearity where the record shows coexisting lineages, and it implies directionality toward the extant form. For most of the last four million years, multiple hominin species were contemporaneous. The present condition of a single surviving hominin species is anomalous within that record, not its natural terminus [1].
